texts.0: SP, due to a cross-check that stopped on the standby heading source while the no-gyro turn commands were being flown, did not hold the assigned pattern and vectoring altitudes until on final. Altitude excursions passed 300 feet from the assigned level and continued to diverge without recognition. The IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the assigned altitude before the aircraft was turned to final.
texts.1: SP, due to a slow altimeter and VVI cross-check between controller transmissions, allowed the aircraft to leave the assigned vectoring altitude. The deviation reached the 300 feet code 1 limit and was arrested only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, with a delayed return to the assigned altitude. No control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch trim setting that was not refined after the configuration change, allowed the assigned vectoring altitude to be lost by approximately 200 to 250 feet. SP detected the trend on the altimeter without prompting and re-established the assigned altitude within 150 feet before the next controller turn instruction. The correction was made with a smooth pitch input and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP held every assigned pattern and vectoring altitude within 150 feet until established on final. Level-offs were anticipated with lead and the altimeter was re-checked immediately after each turn and configuration change. Altitude control was accurate and required no prompting.
texts.4: SP held the assigned altitudes essentially on the assigned level, with excursions of only a few tens of feet, throughout the vectoring pattern. Level-offs were anticipated, trimmed and stabilized before each turn command, and altitude control remained unaffected by the gyro-out workload.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the altitude standards until on final, but the deviations were repeatedly on the low side and settled near the 150 feet band rather than on the assigned level. The pattern shows a tendency to trade altitude for heading control whenever a turn command is received. Earlier trim refinement and a faster return of the eyes to the altimeter after each turn are expected to correct this.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pattern and vectoring altitudes with the IP calling the pitch and power change for each turn command on the first approach and prompting only the altimeter and VVI check on the second. Keeping the altimeter and VVI in the scan through a no-gyro turn command has not yet become an established habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to keep the altimeter and VVI in the scan through every turn command without a call from the IP as the pattern becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP maintained the assigned pattern and vectoring altitude with the deviation settling at the 300 feet code 1 limit, due to a slow altimeter and VVI cross-check between controller transmissions. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the altimeter and VVI in the scan between every controller transmission so the deviation does not reach the 300 feet limit.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the assigned vectoring altitude with the deviation settling between 200 and 250 feet, due to a pitch trim setting that was not refined after the configuration change. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to refine the trim the moment the configuration changes rather than after the deviation shows.
texts_at.3: SP held every assigned pattern and vectoring altitude within 150 feet until established on final, due to one level-off correction applied a beat after the turn rather than with lead. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to anticipate every level-off with lead as consistently as the others.

texts_above.1: SP maintained the assigned pattern and vectoring altitude with the deviation settling at the 300 feet code 1 limit before the level was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP to check the altimeter against the assigned value. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP detected the trend on the altimeter without prompting and re-established the assigned altitude within 150 feet before the next controller turn instruction, correcting the deviation after it had reached between 200 and 250 feet. Refining the trim the moment the configuration changes, rather than after the deviation shows, would keep that trend smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.3: SP held every assigned pattern and vectoring altitude within 150 feet until established on final, anticipating level-offs with lead and re-checking the altimeter immediately after each turn and configuration change. The only refinement available is to apply that same lead to the very first turn as consistently as the later ones. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned altitudes essentially on the assigned level, with excursions of only a few tens of feet throughout the vectoring pattern, anticipating and trimming for each level-off before every turn. There is little left to refine; every level-off is already anticipated rather than corrected into. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude discipline on the vectors.

error_modes.label: Heading control and no-gyro turn response

texts.0: SP, due to an unstabilized bank in the no-gyro turns and a magnetic compass that was read while still turning, did not fly the headings resulting from the controller turn and stop-turn commands. Heading errors exceeded 10 degrees and the aircraft was left displaced from the final approach course. The IP intervened to stop the turn and align the aircraft with the final approach course.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed response to the stop-turn command and an uncorrected roll-out lead, ended the no-gyro turns with heading errors at the 10 degrees code 1 limit. The heading was recovered only after the IP verbally prompted the correction, and the wings-level check was late in each case. The aircraft remained flyable by SP throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to a bank angle that varied between standard and half-standard rate during the turn, rolled out with heading errors of about 7 to 8 degrees. SP identified the error on the magnetic compass after it settled and corrected back within 5 degrees with a small, timely turn before the next controller instruction. No prompting or IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP started and stopped every turn promptly on the controller command, held the required rate throughout, and rolled out with heading errors within 5 degrees. Compass readings were taken only in stabilized flight, and the resulting headings were held steady until the next instruction.
texts.4: SP responded to each turn and stop-turn command without perceptible delay, held an accurate and constant turn rate, and rolled out on headings that were essentially exact. Heading control remained precise for the whole gyro-out approach with no observed hunting.
texts.marginal: SP held the headings within standards, but the roll-outs were consistently a few degrees wide and the corrections lagged the stop-turn commands. The tendency is toward late roll-out lead which will not be tolerable at higher wind or closer to minimums. A firmer, constant turn rate and an earlier roll-out are expected on subsequent rides.

texts_at.0: SP flew the no-gyro turn and stop-turn commands with the IP calling the standard rate of turn on the first command and calling the stop-turn timing for SP to fly on the second. Judging a roll-out lead for a no-gyro stop-turn from timing alone has not yet been learned. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to judge and fly the roll-out lead independently as the timing becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP flew the headings resulting from the controller's turn and stop-turn commands with heading error settling at the 10 degrees code 1 limit, due to a delayed response to the stop-turn command and an uncorrected roll-out lead. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to compute the roll-out lead for every stop-turn command rather than most of them.
texts_at.2: SP flew the headings resulting from the controller's turn and stop-turn commands with heading error settling at about 7 to 8 degrees, due to a bank angle that varied between standard and half-standard rate during the turn. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold a single, constant bank angle through every turn rather than varying it.
texts_at.3: SP started and stopped every turn promptly on the controller command and rolled out with heading errors within 5 degrees, due to one roll-out lead computed a fraction short for the turn rate actually flown. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to compute the roll-out lead from the turn rate actually being flown on every turn.

texts_above.1: SP flew the headings resulting from the controller's turn and stop-turn commands with heading error settling at the 10 degrees code 1 limit before the heading was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the resulting heading. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified the error on the magnetic compass after it settled at about 7 to 8 degrees and corrected back within 5 degrees with a small, timely turn before the next controller instruction, without prompting or IP input. Holding a single, constant bank angle through every turn, rather than varying it, would keep that error smaller. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound turn discipline on the no-gyro vectors.
texts_above.3: SP started and stopped every turn promptly on the controller command, held the required rate throughout and rolled out with heading errors within 5 degrees, with compass readings taken only in stabilized flight. The only refinement available is to compute the roll-out lead from the actual turn rate on every turn rather than most of them. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed turn discipline on the no-gyro vectors.
texts_above.4: SP responded to each turn and stop-turn command without perceptible delay, held an accurate and constant turn rate and rolled out on headings that were essentially exact, with heading control precise for the whole gyro-out approach. There is little left to refine; every roll-out is already exact rather than corrected into. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional turn discipline on the no-gyro vectors.

error_modes.label: Airspeed and configuration control on the approach

texts.0: SP, due to power settings applied without reference to the airspeed indicator during the configuration changes, did not hold the required approach speed. Airspeed excursions passed 20 knots fast and 10 knots slow of the required value, including a decaying trend in the turns. The IP intervened on the power lever to restore the required approach airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to a power change that was not adjusted after gear and flap extension, allowed the airspeed to reach the code 1 boundary of 20 knots fast and 10 knots slow. The excursion was corrected only after the IP called the airspeed, and the return to the required speed was slow and made with a large power input. The aircraft was recovered without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction at the configuration change, allowed the approach speed to build to approximately 12 to 15 knots above the required value. SP recognized the trend and re-established the speed inside 10 knots fast with a measured power adjustment before final. The correction was timely and made without prompting.
texts.3: SP established and held the required approach airspeed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow for the whole approach. Power was set for each configuration change and refined promptly, so the speed remained steady through the turns and on final.
texts.4: SP held the required approach airspeed essentially on value throughout, with excursions of only a few knots at the configuration changes. Power management was anticipatory and the speed was stable from the start of the pattern to minimums.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed within standards, but the value sat consistently on the fast side and drifted toward the 10 knots band whenever attention moved to the turn commands. The trend indicates power that is set once and not refined as drag changes. Anticipatory power setting at each configuration change is expected to tighten this axis.

texts_at.0: SP flew the approach with the IP setting the power for each configuration change on the first approach and prompting the airspeed check on the second. Checking the airspeed indicator the moment power is set at a configuration change has not yet become automatic. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to check the airspeed indicator at every configuration change independently as the sequence becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP established the required approach airspeed with the deviation settling at the code 1 boundary of 20 knots fast, due to power settings applied without reference to the airspeed indicator during the configuration changes. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the airspeed indicator the moment power is set at every configuration change.
texts_at.2: SP established the required approach airspeed with the deviation settling at about 12 to 15 knots above target, due to a late power reduction at the configuration change. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reduce power at the moment of the configuration change rather than a few seconds after it.
texts_at.3: SP established and held the required approach airspeed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow for the whole approach, due to one power adjustment refined a beat after the configuration change rather than with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to refine power together with every configuration change rather than a moment after it.

texts_above.1: SP established the required approach airspeed with the deviation settling at the code 1 boundary of 20 knots fast before the power was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the airspeed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the trend after the deviation built to about 12 to 15 knots above target and re-established the speed inside 10 knots fast with a measured power adjustment before final, without prompting. Reducing power at the moment of the configuration change, rather than a few seconds after it, would keep the excursion smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid power management on the approach.
texts_above.3: SP established and held the required approach airspeed within 10 knots fast and 5 knots slow for the whole approach, with power set for each configuration change and refined promptly so speed remained steady through the turns and on final. The only refinement available is to refine power together with every configuration change rather than a moment after it. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed power management on the approach.
texts_above.4: SP held the required approach airspeed essentially on value throughout, with excursions of only a few knots at the configuration changes and power management anticipatory from the start of the pattern to minimums. There is little left to refine; every power change is already anticipated rather than reacted to. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding power management on the approach.

texts.0: SP, due to descent rate corrections applied in large uncorrelated pitch steps, did not maintain the glide path on the controller advisories. The aircraft went further than 300 feet above and more than 150 feet below the glide path, and the low excursion was still increasing when called. The IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the aircraft on the glide path.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed response to the below glide path advisories, allowed the displacement to reach the limits of up to 300 feet high and up to 150 feet low. The corrections were made only after the IP restated the controller advisory, and each return to the glide path was late and overshot in the opposite direction. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rate of descent that was not adjusted after the initial glide path intercept, drifted to about 200 feet above the glide path before the controller called the trend. SP corrected the descent rate promptly, without prompting, and returned to a slightly above position that the controller acknowledged as on the glide path. The remainder of the descent was flown without further significant displacement.
texts.3: SP intercepted the glide path on the controller advisory and held it within slightly above and slightly below for the whole final. Rate of descent was adjusted in small increments in response to each advisory, and the aircraft arrived at decision height on the glide path.
texts.4: SP flew the glide path with negligible displacement, receiving predominantly on glide path advisories from the controller to decision height. Descent rate was set at intercept and refined with minimal, precise pitch and power inputs.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the glide path within the slightly above and slightly below band, but the aircraft consistently sat on the high side and the corrections were made in larger steps than the advisories required. The tendency is toward a descent rate that is chased rather than set. Establishing the required rate of descent at intercept and correcting in small increments is expected on the next event.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the PAR-flown glide path with the IP flying the pitch and power correction for each below glide path advisory on the first approach and calling the correction for SP to fly on the second. Reading a controller's glide path advisory and converting it into a coordinated pitch and power input has not yet been learned. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to convert each advisory into a coordinated correction independently as the picture becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP tracked the PAR-flown glide path with the displacement settling at up to 300 feet high and up to 150 feet low on separate occasions, due to a delayed response to the below glide path advisories. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to act on a below glide path advisory the moment it is passed rather than after a short delay.
texts_at.2: SP tracked the PAR-flown glide path with the displacement settling at about 200 feet above before it was corrected, due to a rate of descent that was not adjusted after the initial glide path intercept. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to adjust the rate of descent the moment the glide path is intercepted rather than after a controller call.
texts_at.3: SP intercepted the glide path on the controller advisory and held it within slightly above and slightly below for the whole final, due to the rate of descent needing one small refinement after the intercept. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the intercept rate of descent precisely so no refinement is needed afterward.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the PAR-flown glide path with the displacement settling at up to 300 feet high and up to 150 feet low on separate occasions before each was regained. The corrections followed verbal calls from the IP restating the controller advisory. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP corrected the descent rate promptly, without prompting, after the aircraft drifted to about 200 feet above the glide path, and returned to a slightly above position that the controller acknowledged as on the glide path. Adjusting the rate of descent the moment the glide path is intercepted, rather than after a controller call, would remove most of that drift. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to steady glide-path tracking on the PAR-flown approach.
texts_above.3: SP intercepted the glide path on the controller advisory and held it within slightly above and slightly below for the whole final, adjusting rate of descent in small increments in response to each advisory with the aircraft arriving at decision height on the glide path. The only refinement available is to set the intercept rate precisely so no refinement is needed afterward. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate glide-path tracking on the PAR-flown approach.
texts_above.4: SP flew the glide path with negligible displacement, receiving predominantly on glide path advisories from the controller to decision height with rate of descent set at intercept and refined only with minimal, precise inputs. There is little left to refine; the rate is already set correctly at intercept rather than adjusted afterward. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary glide-path tracking on the PAR-flown approach.

texts.0: SP, due to a descent rate that was not reduced approaching the published minimum descent altitude, did not level off at MDA. The aircraft descended below MDA, which admits no negative tolerance, and the level-off was more than 200 feet in error. The IP intervened on the controls to arrest the descent and re-establish the aircraft at the minimum descent altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a late start of the level-off and an altimeter that was not re-checked during the final descent, arrived at MDA with an error at the 200 feet high code 1 boundary and momentarily allowed the altitude to sag toward the published value. The level-off was completed only after the IP called the approaching minimum descent altitude. The aircraft was recovered by SP without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a level-off lead that was not adjusted for the existing rate of descent, stopped the descent approximately 150 to 180 feet above the minimum descent altitude. SP recognized the error without prompting and re-established the aircraft within 100 feet of MDA in time for the missed approach point. No descent below the published minimum occurred at any stage.
texts.3: SP levelled off at the minimum descent altitude within 100 feet high and never descended below the published value. The level-off lead was correct for the rate of descent in use, and the altitude was then held steady to the missed approach point.
texts.4: SP arrived at the minimum descent altitude essentially on value, with a level-off error of only a few tens of feet high and no descent below the published minimum. The altitude was held precisely from level-off to the missed approach point.
texts.marginal: SP respected the minimum descent altitude and stayed inside the tolerance, but the level-off was consistently high in the band and the altitude was allowed to wander before the missed approach point. The trend suggests a level-off lead applied by habit rather than computed from the rate of descent. A lead matched to the actual descent rate, followed by a positive altitude hold, is expected.

texts_at.0: SP flew the level-off toward the minimum descent altitude with the IP flying the pitch and power change for the level-off on the first approach and calling the altimeter check for SP to fly on the second. Timing the level-off from the rate of descent rather than from habit has not yet been learned. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to time the level-off from the rate of descent independently as the picture becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP leveled off close to the minimum descent altitude with the error settling at the 200 feet high code 1 boundary, due to a late start of the level-off and an altimeter that was not re-checked during the final descent. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to re-check the altimeter through the final descent, not only at the level-off itself.
texts_at.2: SP leveled off close to the minimum descent altitude with the error settling at about 150 to 180 feet, due to a level-off lead that was not adjusted for the existing rate of descent. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the level-off lead from the actual rate of descent rather than from habit.
texts_at.3: SP levelled off at the minimum descent altitude within 100 feet high and never descended below the published value, due to the level-off lead being set a fraction short for the rate of descent in use. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to compute the lead from the actual rate of descent on every approach rather than most of them.

texts_above.1: SP leveled off close to the minimum descent altitude with the error settling at the 200 feet high code 1 boundary before the level-off was completed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the approaching minimum descent altitude. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the error on the standby altimeter after it settled at about 150 to 180 feet and re-established the aircraft within 100 feet of MDA in time for the missed approach point, without prompting, with no descent below the published minimum. Setting the level-off lead from the actual rate of descent, rather than from habit, would remove most of that error. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable altitude capture at MDA.
texts_above.3: SP levelled off at the minimum descent altitude within 100 feet high and never descended below the published value, with the level-off lead correct for the rate of descent in use and the altitude then held steady to the missed approach point. The only refinement available is to compute that lead on every approach as consistently as the others. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good altitude capture at MDA.
texts_above.4: SP arrived at the minimum descent altitude essentially on value, with a level-off error of only a few tens of feet high and no descent below the published minimum, holding the altitude precisely from level-off to the missed approach point. There is little left to refine; the lead is already computed rather than estimated. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior altitude capture at MDA.

error_modes.label: Compliance with controller instructions and radio discipline

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology and readbacks that did not match the instruction issued, did not comply with the final controller instructions during the gyro-out approach. Turn, descent and configuration instructions were actioned incorrectly or not at all, and the controller had to repeat the sequence. The IP intervened on the radio and on the controls to restore compliance with the approach instructions.
texts.1: SP, due to transmissions that departed from standard phraseology and readbacks made while the turn was still being flown, actioned several controller instructions late or incompletely. Compliance was achieved only after the IP verbally restated each instruction, and the acknowledgements remained non-standard. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a readback given before the instruction had been fully received, initially mis-set one heading assigned by the controller. SP recognized the discrepancy at the controller repeat, corrected the heading and reverted to standard phraseology for the remaining transmissions. All subsequent instructions were complied with in time and without prompting.
texts.3: SP complied with all ATC and final controller instructions, using standard phraseology throughout the gyro-out approach. Readbacks were accurate and timely, turn and descent instructions were actioned promptly, and no instruction had to be repeated by the controller.
texts.4: SP complied with every ATC and final controller instruction immediately and accurately, with concise standard phraseology maintained under the additional gyro-out workload. Radio work never competed with aircraft control and no clarification was required at any point.
texts.marginal: SP complied with all controller instructions, but several acknowledgements were wordy and delivered while the aircraft was manoeuvring, and one readback needed the controller to confirm. Standards were met, yet the trend is toward radio work that follows the aircraft rather than leading it. Shorter standard readbacks made at stabilized points of the approach are expected on the next event.

texts_at.0: SP complied with the final controller instructions with the IP reading back the first instruction for SP to confirm and prompting each subsequent instruction as it was issued. Recognizing an instruction and actioning it from standard phraseology alone has not yet become consistent under the gyro-out workload. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to read back and action instructions independently as the sequence becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP complied with the final controller instructions with one heading assigned by the controller mis-set initially before it was corrected at the controller repeat, due to a readback given before the instruction had been fully received. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to let the controller finish transmitting before giving the readback.
texts_at.2: SP complied with the final controller instructions with one readback needing the controller to confirm before it was actioned, due to a readback given before the instruction had been fully received. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete the readback only after the full instruction has been received.
texts_at.3: SP complied with all ATC and final controller instructions, using standard phraseology throughout the gyro-out approach, due to one acknowledgement that was slightly wordy while the aircraft was manoeuvring. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep acknowledgements short at stabilized points of the approach as consistently as elsewhere.

texts_above.1: SP complied with the final controller instructions with one heading assigned by the controller mis-set initially before it was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP restating the controller repeat. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the discrepancy at the controller repeat, corrected the heading and reverted to standard phraseology for the remaining transmissions, without IP input, with all subsequent instructions complied with in time. Letting the controller finish transmitting before giving the readback would prevent that discrepancy at the source. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to assured radio discipline on the gyro-out approach.
texts_above.3: SP complied with all ATC and final controller instructions, using standard phraseology throughout the gyro-out approach, with readbacks accurate and timely and no instruction repeated by the controller. The only refinement available is to keep every acknowledgement as short as the others regardless of the manoeuvring in progress. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise radio discipline on the gyro-out approach.
texts_above.4: SP complied with every ATC and final controller instruction immediately and accurately, with concise standard phraseology maintained under the additional gyro-out workload and radio work never competing with aircraft control. There is little left to refine; no clarification is ever required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate radio discipline on the gyro-out approach.

texts.0: SP, due to an approach plate that was not reviewed for the gyro-out pattern in use, violated the routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals. The aircraft was flown below a published segment minimum and outside the protected routing while in the pattern. The IP intervened to re-establish the aircraft on a published routing at a legal altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete recall of the published segment minima, descended to the point at which a published restriction was about to be infringed and remained outside the intended routing longer than briefed. The correction was made only after the IP verbally identified the applicable restriction, and the response was delayed. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a segment minimum that was read late from the approach plate, started a descent early toward a published restriction. SP checked the plate, recognized the discrepancy before the restriction was infringed and re-established the aircraft at the correct segment altitude on the published routing without prompting. No published restriction was violated.
texts.3: SP respected all routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals throughout the gyro-out approach. Segment minima were known in advance, descents were started only at the correct points, and the aircraft remained on the assigned routing.
texts.4: SP flew the approach with full knowledge of the published routing and restrictions, calling each segment minimum before reaching it and descending exactly at the applicable points. Adherence to MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals was maintained without reference difficulty despite the gyro-out condition.
texts.marginal: SP did not infringe any published routing or altitude restriction, but the segment minima were consulted on the plate later than they should have been and one descent was started close to the earliest permissible point. The trend indicates restrictions being recalled reactively rather than briefed. Reviewing the applicable minima before the pattern is entered is expected to remove this margin.

texts_at.0: SP flew the gyro-out approach with the IP identifying the published segment minima on the descent and calling the altitude restriction at each point. SP is expected to identify the segment restrictions from the plate without a call from the IP as the approach becomes familiar.
texts_at.1: SP respected the routing and altitude restrictions with one segment minimum reached at the point it was about to be infringed before it was corrected, due to incomplete recall of the published segment minima. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to review the segment minima before the pattern is entered rather than recalling them in the air.
texts_at.2: SP respected the routing and altitude restrictions with a descent started early toward a published restriction before it was corrected, due to a segment minimum that was read late from the approach plate. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read the applicable segment minimum before starting the descent, not while it is already underway.
texts_at.3: SP respected all routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals throughout the gyro-out approach, due to one segment minimum consulted on the plate a beat later than briefed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to consult every segment minimum at the same point in the briefing as the others.

The correction followed a verbal call from the IP naming the applicable restriction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP checked the plate, recognized the discrepancy before the restriction was infringed and re-established the aircraft at the correct segment altitude on the published routing without prompting, with no published restriction violated. Reading the applicable segment minimum before starting the descent, rather than while it is underway, would remove the need for that recovery. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to competent routing discipline on the gyro-out approach.
texts_above.3: SP respected all routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals throughout the gyro-out approach, with segment minima known in advance and descents started only at the correct points. The only refinement available is to consult every segment minimum at the same point in the briefing as the others. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined routing discipline on the gyro-out approach.
texts_above.4: SP flew the approach with full knowledge of the published routing and restrictions, calling each segment minimum before reaching it and descending exactly at the applicable points despite the gyro-out condition. There is little left to refine; every restriction is already known before the descent rather than recalled during it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless routing discipline on the gyro-out approach.

texts.0: SP, due to spatial disorientation that developed with the primary attitude and heading reference unavailable, did not maintain a usable partial-panel scan during the gyro-out approach. Control inputs followed sensation rather than the standby instruments and the aircraft attitude diverged from the approach profile. The IP intervened on the controls to recover the aircraft and restore instrument flight.
texts.1: SP, due to disorientation cues in the turns that were not resolved against the standby instruments, fixated on single indications and lost the partial-panel scan pattern. The scan was restored only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and control remained coarse in the interim. SP flew the aircraft throughout without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a false turn sensation after a prolonged no-gyro turn, briefly weighted sensation over the standby indications and let bank and pitch become uneven. SP recognized the conflict, referred back to the standby instruments and re-established a full partial-panel scan without prompting, before the approach parameters moved outside limits. Control quality returned to normal for the rest of the approach.

The trend shows disorientation cues consuming attention that the approach needs elsewhere. A more even scan rhythm and an immediate return to the full partial-panel pattern after each turn are expected.
